claim: Oncogenic mutations in KRAS are among the most common in cancer.
source: Oncogenic mutations in KRAS are among the most common in cancer.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data or citation in this sentence.

claim: Loss of epithelial characteristics and the acquisition of mesenchymal traits are associated with cancer aggressiveness and therapy resistance.
source: Classical models suggest that loss of epithelial characteristics and the acquisition of mesenchymal traits are associated with cancer aggressiveness and therapy resistance.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from classical models.

claim: STAT3 is a genetic modifier of TGF-beta-induced epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
source: Here, we identify STAT3 as a genetic modifier of TGF-beta-induced epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gene expression profiling of pancreatic cancer cells identifies more than 200 genes commonly regulated by STAT3 and oncogenic KRAS.
source: Gene expression profiling of pancreatic cancer cells identifies more than 200 genes commonly regulated by STAT3 and oncogenic KRAS.
evidence: This is a direct result from RNA-seq analysis presented in the study.

claim: Functional classification of the STAT3-responsive program reveals its major role in tumor maintenance and epithelial homeostasis.
source: Functional classification of the STAT3-responsive program reveals its major role in tumor maintenance and epithelial homeostasis.
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis of STAT3-regulated genes.

claim: Cancer genomes contain an average of less than five driver mutations.
source: It is estimated that cancer genomes contain an average of less than five driver mutations, whose outcomes are realized in the context of chromosomal and epigenetic alterations (Sondka et al., 2018; Bailey et al., 2018; Consortium ITP-CAoWG, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: STAT3 has tumor-promoting properties that it exerts in a context-dependent fashion.
source: A large body of evidence suggests that signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) has tumor-promoting properties that it exerts in a context-dependent fashion (Yu et al., 2014; Huynh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Canonical activation of STAT3 occurs following phosphorylation of tyrosine 705 (pY705) by receptor-associated Janus kinases (JAKs) or other tyrosine kinases.
source: Canonical activation of STAT3 occurs following phosphorylation of tyrosine 705 (pY705) by receptor-associated Janus kinases (JAKs) or other tyrosine kinases (Philips et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The most common STAT3 mutations, Y640F and D661Y, render STAT3 constitutively active.
source: The most common STAT3 mutations, Y640F and D661Y, render STAT3 constitutively active (Jerez et al., 2012; Koskela et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: STAT3 mutations rarely occur in solid tumors.
source: In sharp contrast, STAT3 mutations rarely occur in solid tumors.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from TCGA data analysis.

claim: Most cancers do not express high levels of activated STAT3.
source: TCGA pan-cancer analysis reveals that most cancers do not express high levels of activated STAT3 (https://www.cancer.gov).
evidence: This is based on TCGA database analysis.

claim: Activation of STAT3 in KRAS mutant cancers led to the stabilization of epithelial differentiation.
source: A previous study from our laboratory uncovered a novel link between STAT3 and cancer showing that activation of STAT3 in KRAS mutant cancers led to the stabilization of epithelial differentiation (D'Amico et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Neither persistent activation of STAT3 nor its loss confers distinct growth advantages on tumor cells.
source: Both in vitro and in vivo assays demonstrate that neither persistent activation of STAT3 nor its loss confers distinct growth advantages on tumor cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from in vitro and in vivo assays presented in the study.

claim: Stabilization of the epithelial phenotype and attenuation of the TGF-β/SMAD4 pathway are two main driving forces behind STAT3 activity.
source: Stabilization of the epithelial phenotype and attenuation of the TGF-β/SMAD4 pathway are two main driving forces behind STAT3 activity (Oft et al., 1996; David and Massagué, 2018; Principe et al., 2021; Gough et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data from the study.

claim: SMAD4 expressing tumors are poorly differentiated and exhibit mesenchymal features only in the absence of STAT3.
source: The data highlight antagonistic epistasis between SMAD4 and STAT3, where SMAD4 expressing tumors are poorly differentiated and exhibit mesenchymal features only in the absence of STAT3, while SMAD4-deficient tumors are well-differentiated and display epithelial morphology only in presence of STAT3.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from tumor morphology studies.

claim: SMAD4-deficient tumors are well-differentiated and display epithelial morphology only in presence of STAT3.
source: The data highlight antagonistic epistasis between SMAD4 and STAT3, where SMAD4 expressing tumors are poorly differentiated and exhibit mesenchymal features only in the absence of STAT3, while SMAD4-deficient tumors are well-differentiated and display epithelial morphology only in presence of STAT3.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from tumor morphology studies.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing was used to generate isogenic STAT3 knockouts in KP MEFs.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing was used to generate isogenic STAT3 knockouts in the KP MEFs, and gain-of-function (GOF) and loss-of-function (LOF) mutant STAT3 alleles were stably integrated into cells via lentiviral vectors (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: STAT3 Y640F, K658Y, and STAT3C displayed increased levels of Y705 phosphorylation.
source: As reported, STAT3 Y640F, K658Y, and STAT3C displayed increased levels of Y705 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Loss of STAT3 expression did not affect cell growth under standard culture conditions.
source: Loss of STAT3 expression did not affect cell growth under standard culture conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on cell proliferation assays.

claim: Loss of STAT3 did not affect KRAS-induced transformation.
source: Likewise, loss of STAT3 did not affect KRAS-induced transformation. This is indicated by the ability of STAT3 KO cells to grow in multilayers and form transformed foci to the same extent as controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on focus formation assays.

claim: STAT3 GOF mutations, Y640F, D661Y, and K658Y, impaired KRAS-induced focus formation.
source: In contrast, STAT3 GOF mutations, Y640F, D661Y, and K658Y, impaired KRAS-induced focus formation (p<0.005 by two-tailed T test, Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on focus formation assays with statistical analysis.

claim: Only a small percentage of cells with hyperactive STAT3 Y640F had some ability to form transformed colonies.
source: Through these real-time studies, we discovered that only a small percentage of cells with hyperactive STAT3 Y640F had some ability to form transformed colonies, while the majority of cells remained contact inhibited.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy observations.

claim: STAT3 S727E had no significant effect on cell transformation.
source: We noted that STAT3 S727E had no significant effect on cell transformation, while the Y640F/S727E double mutant displayed only a marginal increase in the number of transformed foci relative to STAT3 Y640F itself (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on focus formation assays.

claim: The hyperactive Y640F mutation exerts a dominant influence over S727E in KRAS-transformed MEFs.
source: Thus, the hyperactive Y640F mutation exerts a dominant influence over S727E in KRAS-transformed MEFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Y640F and Y640F/S727E double mutant effects.

claim: Lentiviral expression of wild-type or GOF STAT3 alleles, Y640F and D661Y, failed to transform primary p53KO MEFs or immortalized NIH 3T3 cells.
source: As expected, lentiviral expression of wild-type or GOF STAT3 alleles, Y640F and D661Y, failed to transform primary p53KO MEFs or immortalized NIH 3T3 cells (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; data not shown), indicating that STAT3 does not display intrinsic oncogenicity on its own.
evidence: This is based on transformation assays in different cell types.

claim: STAT3 does not display intrinsic oncogenicity on its own.
source: As expected, lentiviral expression of wild-type or GOF STAT3 alleles, Y640F and D661Y, failed to transform primary p53KO MEFs or immortalized NIH 3T3 cells (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; data not shown), indicating that STAT3 does not display intrinsic oncogenicity on its own.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability of STAT3 to transform non-KRAS mutant cells.

claim: Tumors developed by STAT3 KO cells showed growth characteristics similar to those of STAT3 intact vector controls.
source: Tumors developed by STAT3 KO cells showed growth characteristics similar to those of STAT3 intact vector controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on subcutaneous tumor formation assays in nude mice.

claim: Cells expressing the hyperactive STAT3 Y640F and K658Y mutations were delayed in their ability to form tumors in mice.
source: In contrast, cells expressing the hyperactive STAT3 Y640F and, to a lesser extent, K658Y mutations were delayed in their ability to form tumors in mice.
evidence: This is based on tumor formation kinetics in nude mice.

claim: Cell populations with high STAT3 pY705 expression developed tumors more slowly compared to low expressing cells.
source: Following implantation in mice, cell populations with high STAT3 pY705 expression developed tumors more slowly compared to low expressing cells (p=0.005, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on tumor formation assays using FACS-sorted cells.

claim: There is a dose-dependent ability of hyperactive STAT3 Y640F to limit tumorigenicity of KRAS-transformed MEFs.
source: Therefore, there is a dose-dependent ability of hyperactive STAT3 Y640F to limit tumorigenicity of KRAS-transformed MEFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between STAT3 pY705 levels and tumor formation delay.

claim: The frequency of tumor-initiating cells was reduced by approximately ninefold in high STAT3 Y640F expressing cells compared to control cells.
source: Limiting dilution assays in nude mice revealed that the frequency of tumor-initiating cells was reduced by approximately ninefold in high STAT3 Y640F expressing cells compared to control cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on extreme limiting dilution assays.

claim: The DBD mutants of STAT3 Y640F lost the ability to attenuate KRAS-mediated MEF transformation despite their continuous pY705 phosphorylation.
source: Notably, the DBD mutants of STAT3 Y640F lost the ability to attenuate KRAS-mediated MEF transformation despite their continuous pY705 phosphorylation (Figure 2E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on focus formation assays with DNA binding domain mutants.

claim: STAT3 Y640F-mediated inhibition of tumor development and KRAS-induced MEF transformation is dependent on STAT3 phosphorylation at Y705, DNA binding, and gene-specific transactivation.
source: We conclude that STAT3 Y640F-mediated inhibition of tumor development and KRAS-induced MEF transformation is dependent on STAT3 phosphorylation at Y705, DNA binding, and gene-specific transactivation.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with various STAT3 mutants affecting phosphorylation and DNA binding.

claim: Western blot analyses of control and STAT3 Y640F-expressing MEFs showed unperturbed RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling.
source: Western blot analyses of control and STAT3 Y640F-expressing MEFs showed unperturbed RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling (as assessed by phosphorylated ERK1/2 and AKT1), suggesting that STAT3 does not directly alter these downstream KRAS effectors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on Western blot analysis of pathway markers.

claim: STAT3 does not directly alter RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT downstream KRAS effectors.
source: Western blot analyses of control and STAT3 Y640F-expressing MEFs showed unperturbed RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling (as assessed by phosphorylated ERK1/2 and AKT1), suggesting that STAT3 does not directly alter these downstream KRAS effectors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and AKT1.

claim: Expression of STAT3 Y640F in MEFs resulted in the differential expression of approximately 290 genes compared to control cells.
source: RNA-seq analysis showed that expression of STAT3 Y640F in MEFs resulted in the differential expression of approximately 290 genes (p<0.05) compared to control cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Biological processes attenuated by hyperactive STAT3 included differentiation and tissue development, and pathways mediated by TGF-β signaling.
source: Biological processes attenuated by hyperactive STAT3 included differentiation and tissue development, and pathways mediated by TGF-β signaling (Oft et al., 1996; David and Massagué, 2018; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Ablation of the TGF-β signaling components TGFBR2 or SMAD4 in KP MEFs nearly eliminated foci formation and effects of STAT3.
source: Indeed, ablation of the TGF-β signaling components TGFBR2 or SMAD4 in KP MEFs using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing nearly eliminated foci formation and effects of STAT3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on focus formation assays with TGFBR2 and SMAD4 knockout cells.

claim: Hyperactive STAT3 interferes with KRAS-induced transformation through suppression of the TGF-β pathway.
source: The results support the premise that hyperactive STAT3 interferes with KRAS-induced transformation through suppression of the TGF-β pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of TGF-β pathway ablation on STAT3-mediated suppression of transformation.

claim: KRAS mutant cancers tend to fall into two classes based on their canonical KRAS and TGF-β signaling: KRAS-dependent or KRAS-independent.
source: A notable feature of KRAS mutant cancers, including those of the pancreas, colon, and lung, is that they tend to fall into two classes based on their canonical KRAS and TGF-β signaling; those that have a strong dependence on KRAS signaling (KRAS-dependent) or those that have less dependence on canonical KRAS signaling (KRAS-independent; Singh et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: KRAS-dependent tumors have been associated with an epithelial gene signature and morphology.
source: KRAS-dependent tumors have been associated with an epithelial gene signature and morphology, whereas KRAS-independent tumors show enriched expression of mesenchymal genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: KRAS-independent tumors show enriched expression of mesenchymal genes.
source: KRAS-dependent tumors have been associated with an epithelial gene signature and morphology, whereas KRAS-independent tumors show enriched expression of mesenchymal genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pancreatic tumors were detected within 3 weeks following implantation of parental control, STAT3 knockout, SMAD4 KO, or TGFBR2 KO PDAC cells.
source: Pancreatic tumors were detected within 3 weeks following implantation of 104 parental control, STAT3 knockout (KO), SMAD4 KO, or TGFBR2 KO PDAC cells, and there was no statistical difference in tumor latency between the groups.
evidence: This is based on orthotopic tumor formation assays.

claim: There was no statistical difference in tumor latency between parental control, STAT3 knockout, SMAD4 KO, or TGFBR2 KO PDAC cell groups.
source: Pancreatic tumors were detected within 3 weeks following implantation of 104 parental control, STAT3 knockout (KO), SMAD4 KO, or TGFBR2 KO PDAC cells, and there was no statistical difference in tumor latency between the groups.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of tumor formation kinetics.

claim: Tumors in the parental (intact) group were characterized by classical adenocarcinoma-like morphology with glandular structures.
source: Tumors in the parental (intact) group were characterized by classical adenocarcinoma-like morphology with glandular structures (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumor sections.

claim: KRAS KO tumors displayed a highly sarcomatoid morphology indicative of full EMT.
source: In comparison, KRAS KO tumors displayed a highly sarcomatoid morphology indicative of full EMT.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumor sections.

claim: Loss of STAT3 induced a morphological change compatible with EMT.
source: Loss of STAT3 also induced a morphological change compatible with EMT, whereas overexpression of hyperactive STAT3 Y640F resulted in the sporadic co-occurrence of squamous and glandular differentiation.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumor sections.

claim: Overexpression of hyperactive STAT3 Y640F resulted in the sporadic co-occurrence of squamous and glandular differentiation.
source: Loss of STAT3 also induced a morphological change compatible with EMT, whereas overexpression of hyperactive STAT3 Y640F resulted in the sporadic co-occurrence of squamous and glandular differentiation.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumor sections.

claim: Loss of SMAD4 or TGFBR2 was associated with increased epithelial differentiation relative to controls.
source: Loss of SMAD4 or TGFBR2 was associated with increased epithelial differentiation relative to controls.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumor sections.

claim: The TGF-β pathway is a key regulator of tumor cell differentiation and malignant behavior, but not growth rate.
source: This is consistent with previous findings showing that the TGF-β pathway is a key regulator of tumor cell differentiation and malignant behavior, but not growth rate (Izeradjene et al., 2007; Dai et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Comparative RNA-seq analyses of parental KPC control and STAT3 KO cell lines revealed distinct transcriptional profiles that included more than 700 differentially expressed genes.
source: Comparative RNA-seq analyses of parental KPC control and STAT3 KO cell lines revealed distinct transcriptional profiles that included more than 700 differentially expressed genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The enriched genes in KPC parental cells included those corresponding to the major structural proteins in epithelial cells, such as cadherins, claudins, and tight junctions.
source: The enriched genes in KPC parental cells included those corresponding to the major structural proteins in epithelial cells, such as cadherins, claudins, and tight junctions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis.

claim: STAT3 KO cells were enriched in signatures of EMT and embryonic organ morphogenesis.
source: In contrast, STAT3 KO cells were enriched in signatures of EMT and embryonic organ morphogenesis (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Loss of STAT3 is associated with activation of partial rather than complete EMT.
source: The overall pattern of gene expression suggests that loss of STAT3 is associated with activation of partial rather than complete EMT, since epithelial markers (e.g. CDH1 and EpCAM) continue to be expressed, but mesenchymal markers (e.g. FN1 and various collagens) have been acquired (Brabletz et al., 2018; Lambert and Weinberg, 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-expression of epithelial and mesenchymal markers.

claim: STAT3 KO cells had a significant increase in TGFB1, TGFB3 and INHBA expression.
source: Among these genes, STAT3 KO cells had a significant increase in TGFB1, TGFB3 and INHBA expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of TGF-β family genes.

claim: The expression of EMT-activating transcription factors SNAI, TWIST and ZEB was not strongly affected in STAT3 KO cells.
source: The expression of EMT-activating transcription factors SNAI, TWIST and ZEB was not strongly affected, indicating that induction of EMT involves additional STAT3 dependent regulators.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of transcription factor expression.

claim: Induction of EMT involves additional STAT3 dependent regulators beyond SNAI, TWIST and ZEB.
source: The expression of EMT-activating transcription factors SNAI, TWIST and ZEB was not strongly affected, indicating that induction of EMT involves additional STAT3 dependent regulators.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EMT occurs without strong changes in classical EMT transcription factors.

claim: STAT3 and KRAS KO KPC cells displayed similar levels of EMT at the level of gene expression.
source: We computed EMT scores using gene expression values of epithelial (EPI) and mesenchymal (MES) genes. STAT3 and KRAS KO KPC cells displayed similar levels of EMT at the level of gene expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Serresi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on computed EMT scores from gene expression data.

claim: SMAD4 KO cells displayed reduced expression of EMT-related genes.
source: In contrast, SMAD4 KO cells displayed reduced expression of EMT-related genes, while genes involved in epithelial differentiation and RAS dependency were among the most upregulated.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis.

claim: Comparative analysis between STAT3 and KRAS knockout KPC cells revealed approximately 250 STAT3 target genes that were similarly up- or down-regulated.
source: Notably, comparative analysis between STAT3 and KRAS knockout KPC cells revealed approximately 250 STAT3 target genes (>30%) that were similarly up- or down-regulated (Pearson's r=0.88, p<0.00001), suggesting that STAT3 loss partially phenocopies the effects of KRAS inactivation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on comparative RNA-seq analysis with statistical correlation.

claim: STAT3 loss partially phenocopies the effects of KRAS inactivation.
source: Notably, comparative analysis between STAT3 and KRAS knockout KPC cells revealed approximately 250 STAT3 target genes (>30%) that were similarly up- or down-regulated (Pearson's r=0.88, p<0.00001), suggesting that STAT3 loss partially phenocopies the effects of KRAS inactivation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation of gene expression changes between STAT3 and KRAS knockouts.

claim: RAS dependency scores had a significant positive correlation with STAT3 and KRAS expression.
source: Results showed RAS dependency scores had a significant positive correlation with STAT3 and KRAS expression, and a negative correlation with SMAD4 expression (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on computed RAS dependency scores from gene expression data.

claim: RAS dependency scores had a negative correlation with SMAD4 expression.
source: Results showed RAS dependency scores had a significant positive correlation with STAT3 and KRAS expression, and a negative correlation with SMAD4 expression (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on computed RAS dependency scores from gene expression data.

claim: STAT3 is a genetic modifier that can regulate KRAS dependency and tumor development through counterposing EMT.
source: Together these data indicate that STAT3 is a genetic modifier that can regulate KRAS dependency and tumor development through counterposing EMT.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: TGF-β-induced EMT appears to confer adaptive resistance to KRAS inhibition.
source: The apparent antagonism between STAT3 and induction of EMT was of particular interest, as TGF-β-induced EMT appears to confer adaptive resistance to KRAS inhibition (Singh et al., 2009; Hou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: STAT3/SMAD4 and STAT3/TGFBR2 double knockout cell lines formed pancreatic tumors in mice with distinct histological features from single knockouts.
source: DKO cell lines formed pancreatic tumors in mice, but their histological features were distinct from SMAD4 or TGFBR2 single knockouts as they produced mixed epithelial/mesenchymal morphologies with cells expressing both E-cadherin and vimentin (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis and Western blot analysis of tumor markers.

claim: SMAD4 or TGFBR2 intact tumors displayed features of EMT in the absence of STAT3.
source: SMAD4 or TGFBR2 intact tumors displayed features of EMT in the absence of STAT3, whereas SMAD4 or TGFBR2 KO tumors displayed a well-differentiated epithelial phenotype only in the presence of STAT3 (Figures 3A and 4A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumors with different genotypes.

claim: SMAD4 or TGFBR2 KO tumors displayed a well-differentiated epithelial phenotype only in the presence of STAT3.
source: SMAD4 or TGFBR2 intact tumors displayed features of EMT in the absence of STAT3, whereas SMAD4 or TGFBR2 KO tumors displayed a well-differentiated epithelial phenotype only in the presence of STAT3 (Figures 3A and 4A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumors with different genotypes.

claim: Functional antagonism of STAT3 and TGF-β/SMAD4 controls PDAC development and KRAS dependency.
source: The data reinforce the notion that functional antagonism of STAT3 and TGF-β/SMAD4 controls PDAC development and KRAS dependency (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic interaction studies between STAT3 and SMAD4/TGFBR2.

claim: STAT3 and SMAD4-regulated gene signatures demonstrated significant statistical correspondence when aligned with human PDAC samples from the TCGA cohort.
source: When aligned with human PDAC samples from the TCGA cohort (stage I/II tumors), STAT3 and SMAD4-regulated gene signatures demonstrated significant statistical correspondence, supporting the selective antagonism of STAT3 and SMAD4 (Pearson's r>0.5, p<0.00001; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of gene signatures with human tumor data.

claim: STAT3-regulated gene expression is closely associated with epithelial differentiation.
source: Results demonstrate that STAT3-regulated gene expression is closely associated with epithelial differentiation, while SMAD4-regulated gene expression is strongly associated with EMT (Pearson's r>0.7) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis with human tumor samples classified by epithelial/mesenchymal status.

claim: SMAD4-regulated gene expression is strongly associated with EMT.
source: Results demonstrate that STAT3-regulated gene expression is closely associated with epithelial differentiation, while SMAD4-regulated gene expression is strongly associated with EMT (Pearson's r>0.7) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis with human tumor samples classified by epithelial/mesenchymal status.

claim: KRAS-dependent tumors showed enriched expression of epithelial genes and reduced expression of mesenchymal genes.
source: KRAS-dependent tumors showed enriched expression of epithelial genes (EPI) and reduced expression of mesenchymal genes (MES), whereas the KRAS-independent samples displayed the inverse, as previously reported (Singh et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis of human tumor samples with support from citations.

claim: The KPC STAT3 knockout gene signature co-segregated with human KRAS-independent/mesenchymal PDAC tumors.
source: Importantly, the KPC STAT3 knockout gene signature (i.e. upregulated genes) co-segregated with human KRAS-independent/mesenchymal PDAC tumors, while the SMAD4 knockout gene signature (i.e. upregulated genes) co-segregated with human KRAS-dependent/epithelial tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of mouse gene signatures with human tumor classifications.

claim: The SMAD4 knockout gene signature co-segregated with human KRAS-dependent/epithelial tumors.
source: Importantly, the KPC STAT3 knockout gene signature (i.e. upregulated genes) co-segregated with human KRAS-independent/mesenchymal PDAC tumors, while the SMAD4 knockout gene signature (i.e. upregulated genes) co-segregated with human KRAS-dependent/epithelial tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of mouse gene signatures with human tumor classifications.

claim: Liver is the main site of PDAC metastases.
source: Liver is the main site of PDAC metastases, and pancreatic cancer metastases commonly display a stabilized epithelial phenotype (Carstens et al., 2021; Reichert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pancreatic cancer metastases commonly display a stabilized epithelial phenotype.
source: Liver is the main site of PDAC metastases, and pancreatic cancer metastases commonly display a stabilized epithelial phenotype (Carstens et al., 2021; Reichert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The STAT3 transcription factor acts as a genetic modifier of EMT and KRAS dependency in a mouse model of pancreatic carcinogenesis.
source: We provide evidence that the STAT3 transcription factor acts as a genetic modifier of EMT and KRAS dependency in a mouse model of pancreatic carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: STAT3 plays a crucial role in guiding the morphological and functional characteristics of tumors by inhibiting EMT and maintaining epithelial identity.
source: Our results demonstrate that neither persistent activation nor genetic ablation of STAT3 confers a selective growth advantage on tumor cells. Instead, STAT3 plays a crucial role in guiding the morphological and functional characteristics of tumors by inhibiting EMT and maintaining epithelial identity.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations of tumor morphology and gene expression.

claim: The involvement of STAT3 in cancer has been predominantly associated with chronic inflammation and fibrosis.
source: While the involvement of STAT3 in cancer has been predominantly associated with chronic inflammation and fibrosis (Laklai et al., 2016; Ji et al., 2019), our data underscore the significance of epistasis as a key factor that underlies functional antagonism between STAT3 and TGF-β/SMAD4 signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Oncogenic KRAS mutations are observed in approximately 90% of pancreatic cancers.
source: Oncogenic KRAS mutations are observed in approximately 90% of pancreatic cancers and less frequently in other cancer types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KRAS mutation frequency in pancreatic cancer.

claim: The role of KRAS in PDAC maintenance has shown limitations.
source: However, the role of KRAS in PDAC maintenance, once held to be nearly absolute, has shown limitations.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the field.

claim: Cellular morphology (epithelial versus mesenchymal) appears to be one of the most noticeable manifestations of different degrees of KRAS dependency.
source: Cellular morphology (epithelial versus mesenchymal) appears to be one of the most noticeable manifestations of different degrees of KRAS dependency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations in the study and previous literature.

claim: Approximately 50% of moderately to well-differentiated tumors in the TCGA cohort are SMAD4 wild-type.
source: Although SMAD4 classically promotes EMT and KRAS independence (Singh et al., 2009), approximately 50% of moderately to well-differentiated tumors in the TCGA cohort are, in fact, SMAD4 wild-type.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA data.

claim: SMAD4 mutation alone is not sufficient to predispose cancer cells to a particular RAS phenotype.
source: This indicates that SMAD4 mutation alone is not sufficient to predispose cancer cells to a particular RAS phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many well-differentiated tumors are SMAD4 wild-type.

claim: STAT3 sustains the KRAS-dependent phenotype and tumor aggressiveness, with the potential for improved efficacy of anti-RAS drugs.
source: STAT3 sustains the KRAS-dependent phenotype and tumor aggressiveness, with the potential for improved efficacy of anti-RAS drugs, whereas SMAD4 promotes KRAS independence at the expense of enhanced therapy resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional relationship between STAT3 and KRAS dependency.

claim: SMAD4 promotes KRAS independence at the expense of enhanced therapy resistance.
source: STAT3 sustains the KRAS-dependent phenotype and tumor aggressiveness, with the potential for improved efficacy of anti-RAS drugs, whereas SMAD4 promotes KRAS independence at the expense of enhanced therapy resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional relationship between SMAD4 and KRAS independence.

claim: The epistatic relationship between SMAD4 and STAT3 has implications for tumor aggressiveness, metastatic propensity, and therapeutic resistance.
source: Therefore, the epistatic relationship between SMAD4 and STAT3 has implications for tumor aggressiveness, metastatic propensity, and therapeutic resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Large-scale analysis of patient-derived PDACs and pancreatic cell lines reveal low to medium levels of STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation.
source: Large-scale analysis of patient-derived PDACs (n=84) and pancreatic cell lines from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (n=39) reveal low to medium levels of STAT3 Y705 phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of patient samples and cell line data.

claim: Endogenous phosphorylation/activation of STAT3 appears able to function within a narrow operating range in multiple solid tumor types.
source: Endogenous phosphorylation/activation of STAT3 appears able to function within a narrow operating range in multiple solid tumor types.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of low to medium STAT3 phosphorylation levels across tumor types.

claim: There exist KRAS mutant cell lines whose survival and growth are no longer dependent on continued KRAS activity.
source: Further complicating the analysis, there exist KRAS mutant cell lines whose survival and growth are no longer dependent on continued KRAS activity (Ischenko et al., 2021; Muzumdar et al., 2017; Lentsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: STAT3 lacks classical driver properties in vitro.
source: Here, we used genetic analyses to identify STAT3 as a relevant dependency in KRAS-driven cancer. While in vitro evidence indicates that STAT3 lacks classical driver properties, it nevertheless plays an essential role in cancer maintenance and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity.
evidence: This is concluded from the inability of STAT3 to transform cells on its own.

claim: STAT3 plays an essential role in cancer maintenance and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity.
source: While in vitro evidence indicates that STAT3 lacks classical driver properties, it nevertheless plays an essential role in cancer maintenance and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing STAT3's effects on EMT and tumor morphology.

claim: The rarity of STAT3 GOF mutations in human cancers with mutant KRAS may be explained by STAT3's role in cancer maintenance and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity rather than as a classical driver.
source: This may explain the rarity of STAT3 GOF mutations in human cancers with mutant KRAS.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings that STAT3 GOF mutations impair transformation in KRAS mutant cells.
